finding.claim: The /settings/email endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. The state-changing operation runs without any authentication check. Email change is a typical account-takeover step via password reset. Depending on set_email's handling of a None uid, this could write the email on a null/anonymous account or on every row where uid IS NULL. The sibling /settings/password route correctly uses @login_required, which indicates the wrong decorator was applied here.
finding.source: Unauthenticated remote attacker sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, a state-changing account email update

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid') (None if anonymous) and never aborts
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with uid possibly None

finding.guards_checked: login_required exists (line 8) but is not applied to this route. There is no inline check on g.uid in change_email. There is no CSRF protection or re-authentication such as current-password confirmation. No other middleware is present in the file. set_email is a stub, so downstream None handling cannot be verified.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") and never aborts. login_required (8-16) aborts with 401 but is not applied to this route. change_email (36-38) has no inline check on g.uid.
verdict.reason: POST /settings/email (routes.py:34-37) is decorated with login_optional (routes.py:22, which never aborts), so an anonymous request reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37 with no auth check, unlike /settings/password at routes.py:42; the stub set_email (routes.py:48) means the exact downstream impact of a None uid can't be seen, but the missing authentication is real.
